turns.boundedConclusion: The cold-water branch from the main supply to each hot-water storage tank or water heater must have a valve located near the equipment. The valve must serve only that tank or heater, must not interfere with or disrupt the remainder of the cold-water system, and must be accessible on the same floor level as the heater served.

materialChecks.criterion: A valve is required on the cold-water branch from the main supply to each hot-water storage tank or water heater.
The valve must be located near the equipment.
The valve must serve only the hot-water storage tank or water heater and must not interfere with or disrupt the remainder of the cold-water system.
The valve must have access on the same floor level as the water heater served.

forbiddenClaims: Do not replace the requirement that the valve serve only the tank or heater with a mere proximity test.
Do not assert a specific distance for “near” or define access beyond the supplied text.
genuineUnknowns: The provision does not quantify “near” or further define access; a particular installation’s satisfaction of those terms cannot be determined without relevant project facts or applicable interpretive authority.
turns.reasoning: PC 503.1 directly states the branch, valve function, location, system-protection condition, and same-floor-level access requirement. The question asks for the rule, not a project-specific determination.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. A valve that also shuts off another fixture does not serve only the water heater, so proximity to the heater is not enough to satisfy PC 503.1. The rule separately prohibits interference with or disruption of the remainder of the cold-water system.

materialChecks.criterion: The valve must serve only the hot-water storage tank or water heater; serving another fixture fails that condition.
Near-equipment location does not replace the separate serve-only condition.
The valve must not interfere with or disrupt the remainder of the cold-water system.

forbiddenClaims: Do not treat proximity alone as sufficient.
Do not conclude that the hypothetical necessarily causes system disruption beyond the stated fact that the valve also serves another fixture.
turns.reasoning: The hypothetical expressly says the valve also shuts off another fixture, contrary to the requirement that it serve only the heater or tank. The rule’s separate no-interference/no-disruption condition should also be retained without assuming additional facts.

turns.boundedConclusion: PC 504.6 gives the listed requirements for discharge piping serving a pressure relief valve, temperature relief valve, or combination. It specifies both a maximum and a minimum termination height. It allows materials listed in PC 605.4 or materials tested, rated, and approved for this use in accordance with ASME A112.4.1.

materialChecks.criterion: The requirements apply to discharge piping serving a pressure relief valve, temperature relief valve, or combination thereof.
The piping must not be directly connected to the drainage system and must discharge through an air gap located in the same room as the water heater.
The pipe must be at least as large as the valve outlet and discharge full size to the air gap.
The piping must serve a single relief device and must not connect to piping serving another relief device or equipment.
Discharge must not cause personal injury or structural damage, and the termination point must be readily observable by building occupants.
The piping must not be trapped and must be installed to flow by gravity.

The termination must be no more than 6 inches above, and no less than two times the discharge-pipe diameter above, the floor or the waste receptor's flood-level rim. Preserve that stated reference wording; the source does not select a reference for a particular configuration.
The end of the piping must not have a threaded connection; the piping must not have valves or tee fittings.
Permitted materials are those listed in PC 605.4, or materials tested, rated, and approved for such use in accordance with ASME A112.4.1.

The supplied PC 605.4 text identifies water-distribution pipe standards and lists brass, copper or copper-alloy, ductile iron, and specified stainless-steel pipe or tubing standards. Do not imply that the source establishes qualification of an unlisted proposed material without applying the PC 504.6 alternative-material route.

forbiddenClaims: Do not treat the 6-inch maximum as the only termination-height condition; PC 504.6 also states a minimum of twice the pipe diameter.
Do not claim that any particular material qualifies under ASME A112.4.1 without that standard or other applicable qualification evidence.
Do not claim that the listed rules establish whole-system or project compliance.
genuineUnknowns: Whether a particular proposed alternative material has been tested, rated, and approved for this use in accordance with ASME A112.4.1 is not established without facts about that material and the referenced standard.
turns.reasoning: The supplied PC 504.6 text states the discharge-piping conditions directly and incorporates PC 605.4 for one material route. The question asks for the rule, not a project-specific compliance determination.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. One inch above the waste receptor's flood-level rim is below the 6-inch maximum, but for a 1-inch-diameter pipe PC 504.6 also requires at least 2 inches above that rim. The stated 1-inch clearance does not satisfy the termination-height condition.

materialChecks.criterion: For a 1-inch-diameter discharge pipe, the minimum clearance under the stated two-times-diameter rule is 2 inches above the applicable reference.
A termination 1 inch above the waste receptor flood-level rim is below the 6-inch maximum but below the 2-inch minimum; being below 6 inches alone does not satisfy the stated height rule.

forbiddenClaims: Do not conclude the termination-height condition is satisfied solely because the clearance is less than 6 inches.
Do not infer overall project compliance or noncompliance beyond the stated termination-height condition.
turns.reasoning: The correction specifies both the pipe diameter and the measurement reference. Applying PC 504.6's minimum gives 2 inches, so the stated 1-inch clearance fails that height condition regardless of the maximum.

turns.boundedConclusion: The supplied PC 905.4 text is empty, so it states no substantive requirement that can be explained from this record. Its supplied title is metadata and cannot establish a requirement; do not reconstruct one from another code.

Do not reconstruct a requirement from another code or edition.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. The supplied current PC 905.4 record does not establish what an older drawing meant by that section number. The drawing's applicable code, edition, and historical section wording are not supplied.

turns.boundedConclusion: For equipment and appliances installed at grade, MC 304.10 permits either a level concrete slab or other approved material extending at least 3 inches above adjoining grade, or suspension at least 6 inches above adjoining grade. The support must be in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.

materialChecks.criterion: The rule applies to equipment and appliances installed at grade level.
One alternative is a level concrete slab or other approved material extending not less than 3 inches above adjoining grade.
The other alternative is suspension not less than 6 inches above adjoining grade.
The support must be in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.

forbiddenClaims: Do not change either minimum height or describe the alternatives as cumulative requirements.
Do not omit the level condition for the slab/material support or the manufacturer-instructions condition.
turns.reasoning: MC 304.10 states two alternatives, each measured above adjoining grade, and requires the support to accord with the manufacturer’s instructions.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. Exactly 3 inches is not below the slab/material-support minimum of 3 inches; it meets that numerical threshold. That height alone does not establish whole-installation compliance, including compliance with the manufacturer’s instructions.

materialChecks.criterion: The slab/material-support alternative requires an extension of not less than 3 inches above adjoining grade, so exactly 3 inches meets the stated minimum.
The support must be in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions; the stated height alone does not establish that condition.

turns.boundedConclusion: MC 501.3.1 item 3 sets the ordinary environmental-air exhaust distances: 3 feet from lot-separating property lines; 3 feet from operable building openings except in Group U; and 10 feet from mechanical air intakes. Environmental exhaust outlets are not considered hazardous or noxious. The intake-distance exception is limited to the stated same-room, dwelling, or sleeping-unit Class 1 or Class 2 situations and does not waive the property-line or operable-opening distances. Other exhaust categories have distinct requirements. For R-2 and R-3 individual dwelling-unit exhaust, item 6 supplies additional conditions.

materialChecks.criterion: State the item 3 environmental-air distances accurately, including the Group U exception for the operable-opening distance, and identify that the 10-foot distance is from mechanical air intakes.

Preserve both intake-separation exception alternatives: a single room, dwelling, or sleeping unit with less than 750 cfm of Class 1 exhaust; or a single dwelling or sleeping unit with less than 400 cfm of Class 2 exhaust. For either alternative, the sum of energy-recovery-device cross contamination and exhaust re-entrainment through the intake must be less than 10% of intake airflow, as established by the manufacturer.
Make clear that the exception removes only the 10-foot mechanical-intake separation; property-line and operable-opening distances remain applicable.

Keep the other categories distinct: item 1 covers noxious, toxic, explosive, or flammable vapor, fume, or dust ducts and specifies its separate distances; item 2 covers other product-conveying outlets and specifies its separate distances. Do not apply either category's distances as the ordinary item 3 environmental-air rule.

If mentioning non-evaporative heat-rejection or heat-absorption appliance discharge, explain that it is not exhaust and has no required intake separation under the stated rule, but its inlet and discharge must not reduce other exhaust-to-intake separation below required minimums.

Preserve the item 6 scope if discussing R-2 or R-3 individual dwelling-unit exhaust: a dedicated fan may exhaust directly outdoors; kitchen and toilet/bath exhaust may combine at one fan only when serving one dwelling unit; the exhaust must be directed away from a window serving that unit and meet the listed distances to windows, doors, other intakes, and the public sidewalk, as well as items 1 through 5.
Identify that Air Class is to be determined in accordance with ASHRAE Standard 62.1, rather than inventing a classification method from this section.

forbiddenClaims: The intake exception applies at exactly 400 cfm for Class 2 exhaust.
A cross-contamination and re-entrainment value below 10% alone qualifies for the exception, regardless of the applicable flow threshold or served-space condition.
The intake exception also waives the property-line or operable-opening distances.
Environmental-air outlets are subject to the item 1 or item 2 distances merely because those categories appear in the same section.
The section establishes an Air Class without reference to ASHRAE Standard 62.1.
genuineUnknowns: The occupancy and configuration of any actual installation are not provided, so whether the special item 6 R-2/R-3 provisions apply to a particular project cannot be determined.
neededReferences: ASHRAE Standard 62.1, if an Air Class must be determined rather than accepted as an already-established input.
turns.reasoning: The supplied text states the environmental-air distances and the narrow intake exception directly. The strict less-than thresholds and the separate requirement that the combined contamination and re-entrainment be less than 10% must both be preserved. Item 6 is a conditional special regime, not a basis for changing the ordinary item 3 rule.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. Exactly 400 cfm is not less than 400 cfm, so the stated Class 2 alternative is not met. The 5% contamination-plus-re-entrainment figure satisfies the separate less-than-10% condition, but does not cure failure of the flow threshold. The intake-separation exception therefore is not established on these facts.

materialChecks.criterion: Treat the Class 2 threshold as strictly less than 400 cfm; exactly 400 cfm does not qualify.
Recognize that 5% is below the separate 10% combined cross-contamination and re-entrainment ceiling, while explaining that all exception conditions must be satisfied.
Conclude that the exception is not established and that the normal mechanical-intake separation remains applicable; do not suggest the exception waives property-line or operable-opening distances.

forbiddenClaims: Exactly 400 cfm satisfies the Class 2 exception threshold.
The 5% figure makes the hypothetical eligible despite the unmet flow threshold.
Failure of this exception establishes that every other aspect of a particular installation is noncompliant.
turns.reasoning: The hypothetical supplies the relevant served-dwelling context, exhaust class, flow, and combined percentage. The exact boundary fails the text's strict less-than-400-cfm condition, even though the percentage condition is met.

turns.boundedConclusion: MC 505.1 generally requires domestic range hoods and domestic appliances equipped with downdraft exhaust to discharge outdoors through galvanized steel, stainless steel, aluminum, or copper ducts. The ducts must have smooth inner walls, be airtight, have a backdraft damper, and be independent of other exhaust systems; installation must strictly comply with the manufacturer's instructions and the listing. The ductless exception is limited to locations other than Groups I-1 and I-2 and requires a listed and labeled hood, compliance with manufacturer instructions, and otherwise-provided mechanical or natural ventilation under Chapter 4. A separate exception permits Schedule 40 PVC for ducts serving domestic cooking appliances with downdraft exhaust, but only if all five listed installation conditions are met.

materialChecks.criterion: State the outdoor-discharge default and permitted duct materials: galvanized steel, stainless steel, aluminum, or copper.

Preserve the duct requirements: smooth inner walls, airtight construction, a backdraft damper, independence from all other exhaust systems, and strict compliance with manufacturer instructions and the listing.

Limit the ductless exception to locations other than Group I-1 and I-2, and retain all its conditions: listed and labeled ductless range hood, installation in accordance with manufacturer instructions, and mechanical or natural ventilation otherwise provided in accordance with Chapter 4.

Limit the PVC alternative to ducts for domestic kitchen cooking appliances equipped with downdraft exhaust; specify Schedule 40 PVC pipe and fittings and preserve all conditions: installation under a concrete slab poured on grade; trench completely backfilled with sand or gravel; no more than 1 inch above the indoor concrete floor; no more than 1 inch above exterior grade; and solvent-cemented ducts.

forbiddenClaims: The ductless exception applies in Group I-1 or Group I-2.
Any ductless hood qualifies without being listed and labeled or without the specified instructions and ventilation conditions.
The PVC alternative applies to ordinary range-hood ducts generally, rather than the stated domestic downdraft appliances.
The PVC alternative is unconditional or permits omission of any listed installation condition.
genuineUnknowns: The question does not identify a particular hood or duct installation, so project-specific compliance beyond the stated rule is not determined.
neededReferences: MC Chapter 4, if determining whether particular mechanical or natural ventilation satisfies the ductless exception's ventilation condition.
turns.reasoning: The section gives a general outdoor-duct rule and two separate exceptions with distinct scopes. The ductless exception is occupancy-limited, while the PVC exception is limited to domestic downdraft cooking appliances and has five cumulative conditions.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. Group I-2 is expressly excluded from the ductless exception. Following the manufacturer's instructions and having otherwise-provided ventilation do not overcome that occupancy limitation.

materialChecks.criterion: Recognize that the ductless exception is available only in occupancies other than Group I-1 and I-2; therefore the stated Group I-2 facts do not establish eligibility.
Do not treat compliance with manufacturer instructions and otherwise-provided ventilation as sufficient to override the Group I-2 exclusion.

forbiddenClaims: The hypothetical qualifies for the ductless exception because the hood is listed, instructions are followed, and ventilation is otherwise provided.
The Group I-2 exclusion is waived by manufacturer instructions or ventilation.
turns.reasoning: The occupancy limitation is explicit, and the hypothetical identifies the excluded occupancy. The other stated conditions do not displace that limitation.

turns.boundedConclusion: Under FGC 408.4, when a sediment trap is not incorporated into the appliance, one must be installed downstream of the appliance shutoff valve and as close to the appliance inlet as practical. It may be a tee fitting with a capped nipple of any length installed vertically in the tee's bottommost opening, or another device approved as an effective sediment trap. The named exclusions are illuminating appliances, ranges, clothes dryers, decorative vented appliances for installation in vented fireplaces, gas fireplaces, and outdoor grills.

materialChecks.criterion: State the trigger: the requirement applies where a sediment trap is not incorporated as part of the appliance.
State the location as downstream of the appliance shutoff valve and as close to the appliance inlet as practical.

Describe the permitted tee form accurately: a capped nipple of any length installed vertically in the bottommost tee opening; alternatively, another device approved as an effective sediment trap is permitted.

List the stated exclusions without adding others: illuminating appliances, ranges, clothes dryers, decorative vented appliances for installation in vented fireplaces, gas fireplaces, and outdoor grills.

forbiddenClaims: The trap may be installed upstream of the appliance shutoff valve under the stated rule.
Any unapproved device automatically qualifies as an effective sediment trap.
A furnace is among the named exclusions.
A capped nipple of a specified minimum length is required.
genuineUnknowns: No particular installation layout is provided, so what location is as close to a specific appliance inlet as practical cannot be evaluated.
turns.reasoning: The location, alternative forms, and exclusions are expressly given in the supplied section. No additional code source is necessary to state this rule.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. For an ordinary furnace with no incorporated sediment trap, the stated rule requires the trap downstream of the appliance shutoff valve. Placing it upstream does not meet that location requirement.

materialChecks.criterion: Apply the default rule because the hypothetical says the furnace has no incorporated sediment trap and does not identify it as one of the listed exclusions.
Conclude that an upstream-of-shutoff-valve trap fails the stated downstream location requirement.

forbiddenClaims: An upstream trap meets the stated location rule.
An ordinary furnace is among the named exclusions.
The section alone establishes compliance with every other gas-appliance installation requirement.
turns.reasoning: The hypothetical supplies the relevant trigger and proposed location. The specified direction relative to the shutoff valve is unambiguous.

turns.boundedConclusion: Under FGC 406.3.3, when the piping system is connected to appliances or equipment designed for operating pressures below the test pressure, those appliances or equipment must be isolated by disconnecting them and capping their outlets. When gas is energized, the affected piping and joints must be checked with noncorrosive leak-detecting fluid or another approved leak-detecting method.

materialChecks.criterion: Preserve the trigger: the piping is connected to appliances or equipment designed for operating pressures less than the piping test pressure.
State that isolation is performed by disconnecting the affected appliances or equipment and capping the outlet(s), not merely by leaving them connected and closing a valve.
Include the later check: affected piping and joints are checked when gas is energized, using noncorrosive leak-detecting fluid or another approved leak-detecting method.

forbiddenClaims: Closing an appliance valve while leaving the appliance connected substitutes for the stated disconnection-and-capping procedure.
The leak check is optional or must be performed only before gas is energized.
The section supplies a specific test pressure or a complete test protocol beyond the stated isolation and leak-check requirements.
genuineUnknowns: The actual test pressure and equipment operating-pressure ratings are not provided, so whether this trigger applies to a particular installation cannot be determined without those facts.
turns.reasoning: The section directly states the pressure condition, required isolation method, and leak-check timing and methods. It does not state a numerical test pressure.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. Leaving the equipment connected and relying on its closed valve, without disconnection or an outlet cap, does not perform the isolation procedure stated in FGC 406.3.3. The affected piping and joints also remain subject to the stated leak check when gas is energized.

materialChecks.criterion: Conclude that leaving the equipment connected and closing its valve does not meet the stated requirement to disconnect the equipment and cap its outlet(s).
Retain the requirement to check affected piping and joints with a stated leak-detection method when gas is energized.

forbiddenClaims: A closed valve alone performs the procedure stated in this section.
Omitting disconnection and outlet capping is acceptable under the supplied text.
turns.reasoning: The hypothetical expressly omits both required isolation steps. The section provides no alternative permitting a connected appliance to be protected solely by closing its valve.

turns.boundedConclusion: FGC 410.2 sets separate MP-regulator requirements for approval and pressure suitability, reduced outlet pressure under lockup, capacity, access and indoor venting or leak limitation, two instrument-capable tee fittings with different locations and purposes, and a union near the regulator. The stated text requires the downstream tee to be at least 10 pipe diameters from the outlet; it does not describe a gauge as a substitute for that tee or its location.

materialChecks.criterion: The regulator must be approved and suitable for the application's inlet and outlet gas pressures.
The regulator must maintain reduced outlet pressure under lockup (no-flow) conditions; its manufacturer-published capacity must be adequate for the appliances served.
The regulator must have access. If indoors, it must be vented outdoors or equipped with a leak-limiting device; either option must comply with Section 410.3.

A tee with one opening capped or plugged must be between the regulator and its upstream shutoff valve, positioned to permit connection of a pressure-measuring instrument and to serve as a sediment trap.

A separate tee with one opening capped or plugged must be at least 10 pipe diameters downstream of the regulator outlet and positioned to permit connection of a pressure-measuring instrument. A pressure gauge with an isolation valve may also be installed in addition to that fitting.
At least one union must be installed within 1 foot of either side of the regulator. Do not restate this as requiring a union on both sides.

forbiddenClaims: Do not treat the upstream sediment-trap tee and the downstream instrument tee as the same requirement.
Do not state that the downstream tee may be closer than 10 pipe diameters because a gauge is installed.
Do not say the indoor vent or leak-limiting option is unconditional; the text requires compliance with Section 410.3.
Do not claim that the supplied section establishes project-wide compliance.
genuineUnknowns: The supplied text does not give the detailed requirements of Section 410.3.
The supplied text does not establish whether a particular installation satisfies the regulator, appliance-capacity, access, or other project-specific conditions.
neededReferences: FGC 410.3, if the detailed requirements for indoor venting or leak-limiting devices are to be explained.
turns.reasoning: The supplied section expressly states each listed requirement and differentiates the upstream tee's sediment-trap purpose from the downstream tee's instrument-connection purpose. Its downstream minimum is 10 pipe diameters, and it describes the gauge as an additional installation.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. At eight pipe diameters, the downstream tee is short of the stated 10-pipe-diameter minimum. Adding a pressure gauge does not cure that distance; the text permits the gauge in addition to the fitting.

materialChecks.criterion: The required downstream tee must be not less than 10 pipe diameters downstream of the MP-regulator outlet.
A pressure gauge with an isolation valve may be installed in addition to the downstream tee; the text does not provide that gauge as an alternative to the tee or its minimum distance.

forbiddenClaims: Do not say the gauge makes an eight-diameter tee compliant with the stated location requirement.
Do not change the stated 10-pipe-diameter minimum.
turns.reasoning: The supplied text requires the tee itself at least 10 pipe diameters downstream and characterizes the gauge as an additional fitting.

turns.boundedConclusion: BC 1013.1 requires approved exit signs readily visible from any direction of egress travel and sets additional marking requirements where exits or paths are not immediately visible, including marking intervening means-of-egress doors within exits. In exit access corridors and exit passageways, no point may be farther from the nearest visible sign than the lesser of 100 feet and the sign's listed viewing distance. The section lists four exceptions, with the qualifications stated in the text.

materialChecks.criterion: Exits and exit access doors must be marked by an approved exit sign readily visible from any direction of egress travel.

Where an exit or egress path is not immediately visible to occupants, readily visible signs must mark the path to exits and within exits to clearly indicate direction of travel; intervening means-of-egress doors within exits must be marked.
In an exit access corridor or exit passageway, the maximum distance to the nearest visible exit sign is the lesser of 100 feet and the sign's listed viewing distance.
Exception 1: signs are not required in rooms or areas requiring only one exit or exit access.

Exception 2: signs are not required in Group U occupancies or individual sleeping units or dwelling units in Group I-1 or R; however, congregate living units with occupancy exceeding four people must have signs.
Exception 3: signs are not required in dayrooms, sleeping rooms, or dormitories in Group I-3 occupancies.

Exception 4: in Groups A-4 and A-5, signs are not required on the seating side of vomitories or openings into seating areas when signs in the concourse are readily apparent from the vomitories; those vomitories must have emergency egress lighting identifying each vomitory or opening within the seating area.

forbiddenClaims: Do not describe the spacing limit as always 100 feet; the listed viewing distance controls when it is shorter.
Do not omit the conditions or emergency-lighting requirement attached to the Group A-4 and A-5 exception.
Do not treat the listed exceptions as applying to situations beyond their stated categories and conditions.
turns.reasoning: BC 1013.1 supplies both the general marking provisions and the full stated distance formula and exceptions. Applying an exception to a particular project would require facts about its occupancy and layout.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. With a listed viewing distance of 75 feet, the applicable maximum is the lesser of 100 feet and 75 feet: 75 feet. A point 90 feet from the nearest visible sign exceeds that limit, even though it is below 100 feet.

materialChecks.criterion: The corridor distance limit is the lesser of 100 feet and the sign's listed viewing distance.
For a 75-foot listed viewing distance, a point 90 feet from the nearest visible sign exceeds the 75-foot limit.

forbiddenClaims: Do not conclude that being below 100 feet is sufficient when the listed viewing distance is 75 feet.
Do not apply an exception; the hypothetical states that none applies.
turns.reasoning: The stated formula yields a 75-foot maximum. The hypothetical 90-foot distance exceeds it.

turns.boundedConclusion: For ordinary stairs and ramps, handrail height must be uniform and 34–38 inches inclusive, measured above stair-tread nosings or the ramp slope’s finished surface, respectively. Alternating tread devices and ships ladders instead have a uniform 30–34-inch range measured above tread nosings. The stated fitting and bending exceptions permit exceeding the 38-inch maximum only in their specified circumstances; the guard-top alternative is limited to when permitted for stepped or ramped aisles under Section 1029.15.

materialChecks.criterion: State the ordinary 34-inch minimum and 38-inch maximum, the uniformity requirement, and the correct stair and ramp measurement surfaces.
State the distinct 30–34-inch range for alternating tread devices and ships ladders, measured above tread nosings.
Explain that fittings or bendings providing a continuous transition between flights may exceed the maximum height.

Explain that, in Group R-3 occupancies, within Group R-2 dwelling units, and in the specified Group U occupancies associated with them, fittings or bendings may exceed the maximum when used for continuous transition between flights, transition at winder treads, transition from handrail to guard, or at the start of a flight.

State that a guard’s top surface may be used as a handrail along stepped or ramped aisles only where permitted under Section 1029.15; the supplied text does not set a separate numerical height range for that alternative.

When describing the Section 1029.15 guard condition, identify the supplied condition: a guard at the side of the aisle whose top surface complies with the handrail-graspability requirements referenced in Section 1014.3. Do not invent the details of those referenced requirements.

forbiddenClaims: Do not treat 38 inches as exceeding the ordinary maximum; the ordinary range includes 38 inches.
Do not extend the fitting or bending exceptions beyond exceeding the maximum height or beyond their stated uses and occupancy scope.
Do not imply that Section 1029.15 permits the guard-top alternative without its stated aisle and graspability conditions.
Do not supply unstated details of the referenced graspability provisions.
turns.reasoning: BC 1014.2 supplies the measurement points, uniformity requirement, both numerical ranges, and the fitting, bending, and guard-top exceptions. BC 1029.15 supplies the aisle context and guard condition; BC 1014.3 identifies the graspability reference but does not provide its detailed criteria.

turns.boundedConclusion: No. Thirty-eight inches is exactly the ordinary maximum, not more than it. On the stated facts, the fitting and bending exceptions are unnecessary to reach that conclusion.

materialChecks.criterion: Compare the stated 38-inch height with the ordinary maximum of 38 inches and conclude it does not exceed that maximum.
Do not apply an exception that permits exceeding the maximum where the stated ordinary handrail has no special fitting or bending condition.

forbiddenClaims: Do not say that an exactly 38-inch ordinary handrail exceeds the maximum.
Do not make a conclusion about whole-project compliance from the height fact alone.
turns.reasoning: The supplied rule says ordinary handrail height must be not more than 38 inches. The hypothetical gives exactly 38 inches, so it is within the stated numerical limit; that comparison alone is not a whole-system compliance determination.

turns.boundedConclusion: Handrails must return to a wall, guard, or walking surface, or be continuous to the handrail of an adjacent stair flight or ramp run. Where stair handrails are not continuous between flights, they must extend horizontally at least 12 inches beyond the top riser and continue sloping for one tread’s depth beyond the bottom riser. For ramp handrails not continuous between runs, the minimum horizontal extension above the landing is 12 inches beyond both the top and bottom of the runs. Extensions follow the direction of the stair flights or ramp runs. Section 1014.6 provides the listed exceptions, including limited dwelling-unit exceptions, assembly-aisle treatment under Section 1029.15, and alternating-tread-device/ships-ladder rules.

materialChecks.criterion: State the general return-or-continuity requirement: return to a wall, guard, or walking surface, or continue to the handrail of an adjacent stair flight or ramp run.

For stair handrails not continuous between flights, state both the minimum 12-inch horizontal extension beyond the top riser and the sloping continuation for a depth of one tread beyond the bottom riser.
For ramp handrails not continuous between runs, state the minimum 12-inch horizontal extension above the landing beyond both the top and bottom of the ramp runs.
State that stair extensions follow the direction of the stair flights and ramp extensions follow the direction of the ramp runs.
Describe Exception 1 exactly: a handrail within a dwelling unit that is not an Accessible unit, Type B+NYC unit, or Type B unit need extend only from the top riser to the bottom riser.

Describe Exception 2 exactly: a handrail within a Type B+NYC multistory dwelling unit complying with Section 1107.2.5, Items 1 through 3, need extend only from the top riser to the bottom riser. Do not replace that cross-reference with unstated criteria.

State that handrails serving assembly-purpose aisles may comply with Section 1029.15; its supplied text says extensions are not required at the top and bottom of stepped and ramped aisles to permit crossovers within the aisles.

State the alternating-tread-device and ships-ladder exception: handrails may terminate vertically above the top and bottom risers, need not be continuous between flights, and need not extend beyond the risers.

When explaining the assembly-aisle exception, preserve the supplied Section 1029.15 scope: it addresses stepped aisles and ramped aisles exceeding a 1:15 slope, and the stated no-extension condition is to permit crossovers within the aisles.

forbiddenClaims: Do not say that a 12-inch top extension alone meets the stair rule for handrails that are not continuous between flights; the rule separately requires a sloping continuation beyond the bottom riser.

ZR 37-31 gives the broader context that these ground-floor provisions concern certain areas not otherwise governed by ZR 32-30, and states that ZR 37-34 does not apply to qualifying commercial zoning lots under 20 feet wide that existed on both specified dates, or to community-facility buildings used exclusively as a school or a Use Group III(B) house of worship. No property-specific applicability finding follows from that text alone.
